objectives: Draw ray diagrams for reflection and refraction
Explain refraction by a change in wave speed (HT: wavefronts)
Investigate refraction of light through a glass block

questions.q: Describe the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves.
questions.a: Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to it.

questions.q: Write the wave equation. Give the unit of each quantity.
questions.a: v = f λ. v in m/s, f in Hz, λ in m.

questions.q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4.0 m. Calculate its speed.
Put these in order of increasing wavelength: radio, gamma, visible light.
questions.a: Gamma, visible light, radio.

questions.q: Which EM wave is used to take images of broken bones?
questions.a: X-rays.

questions.q: State the law of reflection.
questions.a: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

engage.hook: This pencil is perfectly straight. Why does it look broken where it enters the water?
engage.imageDescription: pencil in a glass of water looking bent at the water surface

reveal.answer: Light from the pencil changes speed and direction as it leaves the water. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so the bottom looks shifted.

learn.heading: Reflection

items: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
Both angles are measured from the normal: a dashed line at 90° to the surface.
Specular reflection: a smooth surface reflects light in one direction, like a mirror.
Diffuse reflection: a rough surface scatters light in many directions, like paper.

learn.imageDescription: ray diagram of light reflecting from a plane mirror with normal and equal angles

learn.heading: Refraction

items: A change in direction when a wave crosses a boundary at an angle.
It happens because the wave changes speed.
Along the normal the speed changes but the direction does not.
Air into glass: light slows down and bends towards the normal.
Glass into air: light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

learn.imageDescription: ray of light refracting through a rectangular glass block with normals and angles labelled

learn.heading: Why waves bend (HT): wavefronts

items: A wavefront joins points on a wave that are in step, like the crests.
When a wavefront meets glass at an angle, one end slows down first.
The other end is still moving fast, so the wavefront turns.
Water waves slow down in shallow water.
The wavelength gets shorter. The frequency stays the same.

learn.imageDescription: car driving at an angle from smooth road onto mud, one wheel slowing first, as an analogy for refraction

build.q: A ray hits a plane mirror at 35° to the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
build.explanation: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.

build.q: Light passes from air into glass at an angle. What happens to it?
options: It speeds up and bends away from the normal
It slows down and bends away from the normal
It speeds up and bends towards the normal
It slows down and bends towards the normal
build.explanation: Glass slows light down, so it bends towards the normal.

build.q: Which surface gives diffuse reflection?
build.explanation: Paper is rough on a tiny scale, so it scatters light in many directions.

build.q: A ray enters the glass block along the normal. What happens to it?
options: It bends away from the normal
It goes straight on without bending
It reflects back along the normal
build.explanation: It slows down, but the whole wavefront slows at once, so the direction does not change.

build.q: Where do you measure the angle of refraction?
options: Between the refracted ray and the normal
Between the refracted ray and the block
Between the incident and refracted rays
Between the incident ray and the normal
build.explanation: All ray angles are measured from the normal.

build.q: What is the best way to record the path of a ray?
options: Draw along the ray with a pen
Mark two crosses far apart, then join them with a ruler
Estimate it after removing the ray box
build.explanation: Crosses far apart give an accurate straight line and a more accurate angle.

build.title: Refraction through a glass block
build.intro: Trace rays through a glass block and off a mirror, and measure the angles from the normal.
equipment: ray box, slit and power supply
steps: Draw around the block. Draw a dashed normal at 90° to one long side.
Shine a single ray at the normal at an angle. Mark the rays in and out with crosses.
Remove the block. Join the crosses to draw the ray through the block.
Measure the angles of incidence and refraction. Repeat for three angles.
Swap the block for the mirror. Measure the angles of incidence and reflection.
build.warning: Ray box bulbs get hot. The room is dim: keep bags and stools tucked in.
build.imageDescription: light ray from a ray box passing through a rectangular glass block on paper

questions.q: What happened to the ray as it entered the glass?
questions.a: It slowed down and bent towards the normal: the angle of refraction was smaller than the angle of incidence.

questions.q: What happened as the ray left the glass?
questions.a: It sped up and bent away from the normal. It left parallel to the ray that went in.

developing.q: Draw a ray diagram of light reflecting off a plane mirror. Label the normal and both angles.
developing.a: Incident and reflected rays at equal angles to a dashed normal. Angles of incidence and reflection labelled.
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
A change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary at an angle, caused by a change in speed.

reaching.q: Describe what happens to a ray of light as it enters and leaves a glass block at an angle.
reaching.a: Entering: slows down, bends towards the normal. Leaving: speeds up, bends away from the normal.

reaching.q: Explain the difference between specular and diffuse reflection.
reaching.a: Specular: a smooth surface reflects light in one direction. Diffuse: a rough surface scatters light in many directions.

reaching.q: A ray hits glass along the normal. Describe what happens and explain why.
reaching.a: It goes straight on. It slows down, but the whole wavefront slows at once, so its direction does not change.

mastering.q: (HT) Use wavefronts to explain why light bends towards the normal as it enters glass.
mastering.a: One end of the wavefront enters the glass first and slows down. The rest is still fast, so the wavefront turns towards the normal.

mastering.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air (3.0 × 10^8 m/s) travels at 2.0 × 10^8 m/s in glass. Find its wavelength in glass.
mastering.given: λ in air = 600 nm, v in air = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s, v in glass = 2.0 × 10^8 m/s
mastering.equation: v = f λ (f stays the same)

mastering.q: A fish looks shallower than it really is to someone on the bank. Explain why.
mastering.a: Light from the fish speeds up as it leaves the water and bends away from the normal. The eye traces it back in a straight line, to a higher point.

objectives: Name the parts of animal and plant cells and what they do
Prepare and look at an onion cell slide

questions.q: Name the part of the microscope you look through.
questions.a: The eyepiece (lens).

questions.q: Which objective lens should you start with: the lowest or the highest power?
questions.a: The lowest power.

questions.q: What does magnify mean?
questions.a: To make something look bigger than it really is.

questions.q: Name two of the seven life processes.
questions.a: Any two: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition.

questions.q: What is the unit of force?
questions.a: The newton (N).

questions.q: Name the force that acts when two surfaces rub together.
questions.a: Friction.

engage.hook: These blue shapes were scraped from the inside of someone's mouth. What are they?
engage.imageDescription: human cheek cells stained blue under a light microscope

reveal.answer: Cheek cells, stained blue so they show up. Every part of you is made of cells like these. The dark dot in each one is the nucleus.

learn.heading: Parts of an animal cell

items: Nucleus: controls the cell. Contains the genetic material.
Cell membrane: controls what goes in and out of the cell.
Cytoplasm: a jelly where chemical reactions happen.
Mitochondria: where respiration releases energy.

learn.imageDescription: simple animal cell diagram with nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane

learn.heading: Extra parts in a plant cell

items: Cell wall: made of cellulose. Strengthens and supports the cell.
Permanent vacuole: filled with cell sap. Keeps the cell firm.
Chloroplasts: absorb light for photosynthesis.
Nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm and mitochondria.

learn.imageDescription: labelled plant cell with cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuole and chloroplasts

build.q: Which part controls what the cell does?
build.explanation: The nucleus holds the genetic material that controls the cell.

build.q: Where in the cell does respiration happen?
build.explanation: Mitochondria release energy by respiration. Chloroplasts do photosynthesis.

build.q: Which part is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
build.explanation: Only plant cells have a cell wall. Both have a membrane, nucleus and cytoplasm.

build.q: Why do we add iodine to the onion skin?
options: To stain the cells so parts show up
To stop the cells drying out
build.explanation: Iodine stains the cells, so the nucleus and cell wall are easier to see.

build.q: Why do you lower the cover slip at an angle?
options: To stop air bubbles getting trapped
build.explanation: Lowering it slowly at an angle pushes the air out.

build.q: Which objective lens do you start with?
build.explanation: The lowest power is easiest to focus and shows the most of the slide.

build.title: Looking at onion cells
build.intro: Make a slide of onion skin, stain it and draw what you see.
steps: Peel a thin layer of skin from the inside of the onion with tweezers.
Lay it flat on the slide. Add 2 drops of iodine solution.
Lower the cover slip slowly at an angle to keep out air bubbles.
Start on the lowest power and focus. Draw a few cells in pencil.
Put used slides in the discard pot.
build.warning: Iodine stains skin and clothes. Cover slips are thin glass: tell your teacher if one breaks.
build.imageDescription: steps to make an onion cell slide: onion, peeling skin, adding iodine, lowering cover slip

questions.q: Which parts of the cell could you see?
questions.a: The cell wall, cytoplasm and nucleus.

questions.q: Why could you not see any chloroplasts?
questions.a: Onion bulb cells grow underground with no light, so they have no chloroplasts.

developing.q: Draw an onion cell from your slide. Label the cell wall, cytoplasm and nucleus.
developing.a: A box-shaped cell drawn in pencil, with ruled label lines to the cell wall, cytoplasm and nucleus.

developing.q: Name the part of the cell that controls what the cell does.
Name three parts found in both animal and plant cells.
developing.a: Any three: nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria.

reaching.q: Give the job of the cell membrane and of the mitochondria.
reaching.a: Cell membrane: controls what goes in and out. Mitochondria: respiration releases energy.

reaching.q: Name three parts found only in plant cells. Give the job of each.
reaching.a: Cell wall: support. Permanent vacuole: holds cell sap and keeps the cell firm. Chloroplasts: photosynthesis.

reaching.q: Why could you not see chloroplasts in your onion cells?
reaching.a: Onion bulb cells grow underground with no light, so they have no chloroplasts.

mastering.q: Compare animal and plant cells. Give what is the same and what is different.
mastering.a: Both have a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and mitochondria. Only plant cells have a cell wall, a permanent vacuole and chloroplasts.
starters: Both animal and plant cells have

mastering.q: A leaf cell has many chloroplasts. A root cell has none. Suggest why.
mastering.a: Leaves get light, so they photosynthesise. Roots are underground with no light, so chloroplasts would be no use.

mastering.q: Write the steps to make an onion cell slide. Say how to avoid air bubbles.
mastering.a: Peel thin onion skin, lay it flat on a slide, add iodine, lower the cover slip at an angle to keep out bubbles, view on lowest power.

cloze: The _____ controls what the cell does.
The _____ controls what goes in and out of the cell.
Plant cells have a _____ made of cellulose for support.

objectives: Explain how electron microscopes increased our understanding of cells

questions.q: Write the equation for magnification.
questions.a: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object

questions.q: An image is 5 mm long. The real cell is 0.05 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
questions.hint: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object

questions.q: Which part of a light microscope do you turn to focus the image?
questions.a: The focusing knob (coarse, then fine focus).

questions.q: Why do you start with the lowest power objective lens?
questions.a: It has the widest field of view, so the cells are easier to find and focus.

questions.q: Name two structures found in plant cells but not in animal cells.
questions.a: Any two: cell wall, chloroplasts, permanent vacuole.

questions.q: Why is iodine added to an onion cell slide?
questions.a: It stains the cells so structures like the nucleus show up.

engage.hook: This bacterium is about 2 µm long. Could a school microscope show it in this much detail?
engage.imageDescription: electron micrograph of E. coli bacteria dividing

reveal.answer: No. This was taken with an electron microscope. A school light microscope shows a bacterium as a tiny blob with no detail inside.

rows.a: Can show living cells, in colour
rows.b: Specimens are dead; images are black and white

rows.a: Cheap, small and easy to carry
rows.b: Expensive, very large, needs a vacuum

learn.heading: Magnification and resolution

items: Magnification: how many times bigger the image is than the real object.
Resolution: the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate.
Higher resolution shows much finer detail.
Scientists could now see ribosomes and the inside of mitochondria and chloroplasts.
This increased our understanding of sub-cellular structures.

learn.imageDescription: transmission electron microscope in a laboratory

learn.heading: Biological drawings

items: Pencil only, with clear single lines. No shading.
Draw only what you see, large: at least half a page.
Label lines drawn with a ruler. Label lines never cross.
A title.
The magnification used.

learn.imageDescription: example biological drawing of onion epithelial cells with ruled labels, title and magnification

build.q: Which of these gives the highest resolution?
build.explanation: Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so the resolution is much higher.

build.q: What is resolution?
options: How many times bigger the image is
The smallest distance between two points seen as separate
How wide the field of view is
build.explanation: Magnification is how much bigger. Resolution is how much detail.

build.q: Which structure can only be seen with an electron microscope?
build.explanation: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across, far below the 200 nm resolution of a light microscope.

build.q: Which is correct for a biological drawing?
options: Draw in pen so the lines are clear
Draw in pencil with clear single lines
build.explanation: Pencil, single clear lines, no shading, and only what you see.

build.q: How should label lines be drawn?
options: With a ruler, and they must not cross
With arrowheads pointing at the part
In a different colour for each part
build.explanation: Straight ruled lines that never cross keep the drawing clear.

build.q: A cell's image is 20 mm long at ×400. What is its real length?
build.explanation: real size = image size ÷ magnification = 20 ÷ 400 = 0.05 mm.

build.title: Biological drawing from a slide
build.intro: Draw cells from a prepared slide, following the rules for biological drawings.
steps: Put a slide on the stage. Focus on the lowest power objective first.
Turn to a higher power. Refocus with the fine focus knob.
Draw 2 or 3 cells large, in pencil, with single clear lines.
Label with ruled lines. Add a title and the magnification.
build.warning: Never let the objective lens touch the slide. Carry microscopes with two hands.
build.imageDescription: light microscope with stage, objective lenses and focusing knobs

questions.q: What magnification did you use? Show how you worked it out.
questions.a: Eyepiece × objective, e.g. ×10 × ×40 = ×400.

questions.q: Name two structures you could not see. Explain why.
questions.a: e.g. ribosomes and the inside of mitochondria: smaller than the resolution of a light microscope.

developing.q: Give two differences between light and electron microscopes.
developing.a: Electron: higher magnification and higher resolution. Light: can show living cells and is cheaper.

developing.q: Give three rules for a good biological drawing.
developing.a: Any three: pencil; single clear lines; no shading; large; ruled label lines that do not cross; title; magnification.
How many times bigger the image is than the real object.

reaching.q: A cell's image is 15 mm long. The real cell is 0.03 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
reaching.equation: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object

reaching.q: Explain why a light microscope cannot show ribosomes.
reaching.a: Ribosomes are smaller than the resolution of a light microscope (about 200 nm), so they cannot be seen as separate.

reaching.q: Explain how electron microscopes increased our understanding of cells.
reaching.a: Much higher resolution and magnification show finer detail, so sub-cellular structures like ribosomes and the inside of mitochondria were seen.

mastering.q: A mitochondrion is 2 µm long. In a micrograph it is 40 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
mastering.equation: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object

mastering.q: A bacterium is 0.002 mm long. Give this length in µm, and in mm in standard form.
A scientist wants to watch a living white blood cell engulf bacteria. Which microscope should they use? Explain.
mastering.a: A light microscope. Electron microscope specimens are dead, in a vacuum. A light microscope can show living cells moving.

objectives: Draw the resultant of two waves graphically
Explain constructive and destructive interference using phase difference

questions.q: Define the amplitude of a wave.
questions.a: The maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

questions.q: Define phase difference.
questions.a: The difference in displacement between particles along a wave, or between two waves, in degrees or radians.

questions.q: Define the intensity of a wave and give its unit.
questions.a: The power per unit area at right angles to the wave. W m^-2.

questions.q: A wave has intensity 4.0 W m^-2. Its amplitude doubles. What is the new intensity?
questions.a: I \propto A^2, so 4 × 4.0 = 16 W m^-2

questions.q: What happens to the wavelength of light when it enters glass from air?
questions.a: It decreases. The speed falls and the frequency stays the same.

questions.q: State the speed of all EM waves in a vacuum.

engage.hook: Noise-cancelling headphones make their own sound to make things quieter. How can adding sound reduce noise?
engage.imageDescription: passenger wearing noise-cancelling headphones on an aeroplane
engage.prompt: Discuss with the person next to you. We come back to this at the end.

learn.heading: The principle of superposition

items: When two waves of the same type meet, they superpose.
The resultant displacement at a point is the sum of the individual displacements.
Displacement is a vector: up is positive, down is negative.
The waves pass through each other unchanged.

learn.imageDescription: two pulses before, during and after superposing, with the combined pulse A+B

learn.heading: Constructive and destructive interference

items: Waves in phase: phase difference 0 (or 360°, 2π rad).
Peak meets peak: resultant amplitude = A_1 + A_2.
Waves in antiphase: phase difference 180° (π rad).
Peak meets trough: resultant amplitude = A_1 − A_2.
Equal amplitudes cancel completely.

learn.imageDescription: two waves in phase adding to a large resultant, and two waves in antiphase cancelling

learn.heading: Drawing the resultant

items: Draw both waves on the same axes.
At regular points, add the two displacements, keeping their signs.
Plot the sums and join them with a smooth curve.
I \propto A^2, so doubling the resultant amplitude gives 4 times the intensity.

learn.imageDescription: two waves of different wavelengths and the non-sinusoidal resultant wave below them

build.q: Two pulses with displacements +3 cm and −1 cm meet. What is the resultant displacement?
build.explanation: Add with signs: 3 + (−1) = +2 cm.

build.q: Two waves are in antiphase. What is their phase difference?
build.explanation: Antiphase: one is at a peak when the other is at a trough, 180° or π rad.

build.q: Waves of amplitude 3 mm and 5 mm meet in antiphase. What is the resultant amplitude?
build.explanation: Antiphase: subtract, 5 − 3 = 2 mm.

build.q: What happens to two waves after they have superposed?
build.explanation: Waves pass through each other. Superposition only happens where they overlap.

build.q: The resultant amplitude is double the amplitude of one wave. What happens to the intensity?
build.explanation: I \propto A^2, so 2^2 = 4 times.

build.q: Which two waves cancel completely?
build.explanation: Equal amplitudes in antiphase give zero resultant displacement everywhere.

worked.prompt: A 2.0 cm wave (intensity 3.0 W m^-2) meets a 1.0 cm wave in phase. Find the resultant intensity.

yourTurn.prompt: The same two waves now meet in antiphase. Find the resultant intensity.

statements.text: When two waves cancel, they are destroyed.
statements.correction: They pass through each other unchanged. They only cancel where they overlap.

statements.text: Superposition only works for light waves.
statements.correction: It works for any two waves of the same type: sound, water, light, waves on strings.

statements.text: A resultant displacement can be smaller than either wave's displacement.
Doubling the amplitude doubles the intensity.
statements.correction: I \propto A^2, so doubling the amplitude gives 4 times the intensity.

statements.text: Waves in phase have a phase difference of 0 or 2π rad.

developing.a: When two waves meet, the resultant displacement at a point is the sum of the individual displacements.

developing.q: Pulses of +4 cm and −1 cm meet. Find the resultant displacement.
What is meant by two waves being in antiphase?
developing.a: Phase difference of 180° (π rad): one is at a peak when the other is at a trough.

reaching.q: Sketch two waves in phase and their resultant. Label the amplitudes.
reaching.a: Resultant has the same wavelength, in phase with both, amplitude = sum of the two amplitudes.

reaching.q: Waves of amplitude 4 mm and 6 mm meet. Find the largest and smallest possible resultant amplitudes.
Explain how noise-cancelling headphones reduce noise.
reaching.a: They make sound in antiphase with the noise, at the same amplitude. Superposition gives destructive interference, so the resultant is near zero.

mastering.q: A 3.0 mm wave has intensity 9.0 W m^-2. It meets an identical wave in phase. Find the resultant intensity.
Two identical waves cancel completely at a point. Explain why energy is not destroyed.
mastering.a: Energy is redistributed. Where the waves cancel the intensity is zero, but where they reinforce it is 4 times one wave's intensity.

mastering.q: Sketch the resultant of a wave (λ = 4 cm, A = 2 cm) and a wave (λ = 8 cm, A = 3 cm) starting together.
mastering.a: Add displacements at regular points. The resultant is not a sine wave and repeats every 8 cm.
